name: Salt-Rising Bread
description: Historical recipe from Canadian Farm Cook Book (1911). Source method; not modernized or kitchen-tested.

ingredients.name: 1/2 pint fresh sweet milk or warm water
ingredients.originalText: 1/2 pint fresh sweet milk or warm water
ingredients.quantityText: 1/2 pint fresh sweet milk or warm water

instructions.text: Pour half a pint of water on 2 tablespoons of cornmeal and a generous pinch of salt.
Let it stand for 10 minutes, then stir in 2 tablespoons of flour and set it in a warm place to rise over night.
In the morning add half a pint of fresh, sweet milk, or warm water — either must be lukewarm — and just flour enough to make the yeast smooth.
Put the vessel containing it in a pan or kettle of hot water, hot enough to bear your hand in and be very careful to keep it the same temperature.
When this rises pour it into a batter made of 2 quarts of fresh morning's milk, scalded, then cooled to lukewarm, and mixed with flour enough to make a batter.
Beat this well, using a long spoon, then set the whole to rise again in a warm place.
This will be about twenty-five or thirty minutes if it has been well managed.
Now stir in enough flour to make a batter so stiff it cannot be stirred with a spoon.
Turn it out on a moulding board well dredged with flour, and before kneading it add a piece of lard the size of a large apple.
Mix this well into the dough.

source.originalInstructions:
1. Pour half a pint of water on 2 tablespoons of cornmeal and a generous pinch of salt.
2. Let it stand for 10 minutes, then stir in 2 tablespoons of flour and set it in a warm place to rise over night.
3. In the morning add half a pint of fresh, sweet milk, or warm water — either must be lukewarm — and just flour enough to make the yeast smooth.
4. Put the vessel containing it in a pan or kettle of hot water, hot enough to bear your hand in and be very careful to keep it the same temperature.
5. When this rises pour it into a batter made of 2 quarts of fresh morning's milk, scalded, then cooled to lukewarm, and mixed with flour enough to make a batter.
6. Beat this well, using a long spoon, then set the whole to rise again in a warm place.
7. This will be about twenty-five or thirty minutes if it has been well managed.
8. Now stir in enough flour to make a batter so stiff it cannot be stirred with a spoon.
9. Turn it out on a moulding board well dredged with flour, and before kneading it add a piece of lard the size of a large apple.
10. Mix this well into the dough.
